editorial.headline: The Arena as a Business: KBLI 93113
editorial.standfirst: A broad sports-facilities activity, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium—though each Bali address still needs verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 93113 is about providing the venue and facility itself for sport: an indoor or outdoor setting for land, water and air activities. Its scope is intentionally wide, reaching from facilities for swimming and bowling to arenas for ice hockey, bungee jumping and winter sports. It also expressly includes arenas for slingshot activities, paragliding and hang gliding. The point of connection is not a single sporting discipline; it is the management of the place and the facilities in which those activities occur. That makes this a classification with an unusually broad physical canvas, spanning water, ground and air, while remaining centred on the operation of an arena or facility.

For a business choosing this activity, its principal activity is the provision and management of those sports venues and facilities. The examples help give the term arena its working shape: it can be a swimming venue, a bowling arena, an ice-hockey arena, a bungee-jumping facility, a winter-sports venue, or a site for paragliding or hang gliding. The record opens the activity to Menengah and Besar scales. In editorial terms, this is a category defined by the operating facility—not by an abstract association with sport. The facility is the business’s centre of gravity, and its management is identified as the principal activity.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is straightforward. KBLI 93113 is TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain English, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this defined activity; there is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership in the record. That clarity applies to the activity as described—providing and managing the listed kinds of sports venues and facilities—and it should not be blurred by the separate provincial lens that applies in Bali.

Bali needs that separate reading. Here this activity is recorded as medium-high/high risk, and the consequence is material: it is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium. The provincial rule is described as island-wide and permanent, blocking PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. That description does not extend the block to this activity. But “not blocked” is not the same thing as a generic, location-free conclusion. The Bali note expressly says to verify per address. So the honest Bali position is precise: the moratorium does not bar this medium-high/high-risk activity, while the particular address still requires verification. National openness is real, and Bali’s pathway remains address-specific.
